content:
In a major boost to India's ITIs ecosystem, Shareholders' Agreements (SHAs) have been signed under the Pradhan Mantri Skilling and Employability Transformation through Upgraded ITIs (PM-SETU) scheme for the upgradation of Government Industrial Training Institutes (ITIs) in Gujarat and Andhra Pradesh through a partnership with ArcelorMittal Nippon Steel India (AM/NS India).
The agreements have been signed between the Directorate General of Training (DGT), Ministry of Skill Development and Entrepreneurship (MSDE), Government of India, the Governments of Gujarat and Andhra Pradesh, and AM/NS India, paving the way for the implementation of approved Strategic Investment Plans (SIPs) in the two states for the said two clusters.
The partnership covers a cluster of five Government ITIs in Surat, Gujarat, and a cluster of four Government ITIs in Visakhapatnam, Andhra Pradesh, marking another important milestone in the implementation of PM-SETU, which seeks to transform India's ITI ecosystem through deep industry participation and world-class training infrastructure.
The signing of the SHAs formally establishes the framework through which the industry partner, the Government of India and the respective State Governments will work together to implement the approved projects. Dedicated Special Purpose Vehicles (SPVs) will now be established to manage the upgradation and operations of the ITI clusters, with AM/NS India holding a 51% stake, while the Government of India and the respective State Governments will each hold 24.5% equity participation.
Speaking on the event, Smt. Debashree Mukherjee, Secretary, Ministry of Skill Development and Entrepreneurship, said: “The signing of these agreements is not the finish line, but the starting point of a transformative journey for our ITIs. As India secured a place among the Top 10 in world's leading performers at WorldSkills competition held in Shanghai recently, we must now aspire for PM-SETU institutions and Aspirational Institutes to become centres of excellence that nurture future WorldSkills champions. Our goal is not only to upgrade infrastructure, but to elevate aspirations, quality and outcomes across the skilling ecosystem”.
Industry-Academia Collaboration for Future-Ready Skills
AM/NS India will implement the project in collaboration with New Age Makers' Institute of Technology (NAMTECH), its academic and technical partner. While AM/NS India will contribute its extensive manufacturing expertise and industry insights, NAMTECH will support curriculum enhancement, training delivery reforms, faculty development and academic innovation.
The planned interventions include:
Modernisation of training infrastructure, workshops and laboratories;
Introduction of new-age, industry-relevant trades and technologies;
Upgradation of existing curricula to align with emerging industry requirements;
Strengthening instructor training and capacity building;
Expansion of hands-on, practical learning opportunities for trainees.
These interventions are expected to significantly improve training quality, employability outcomes and industry readiness among ITI graduates.
Major Industry Commitment Under PM-SETU
The Surat and Visakhapatnam clusters together account for an approved investment of approximately ₹440 crore, including ₹240 crore for the Surat cluster and ₹200 crore for the Visakhapatnam cluster.
Notably, the AM/NS India-led projects represent one of the largest industry commitments approved under PM-SETU so far from a total approved amount of ₹3,446 crore proposed investment across the first 14 Strategic Investment Plans (SIPs) under the scheme.
About PM-SETU
PM-SETU is a flagship scheme of the Government of India with a total outlay of ₹60,000 crore, aimed at transforming the country's vocational education ecosystem through strong industry partnerships and institutional reforms. The scheme envisages the upgradation of 1,000 Government ITIs across the country and the strengthening of five National Skill Training Institutes (NSTIs).

title: From Addiction to Independence
subtitle: Gorakhpur UP’s Imran Khan’s Journey Towards a Drug-Free Life
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                12 OCT 2026 6:26PM by PIB Delhi
content:
Timely access to medical treatment, counselling and rehabilitation can help individuals recover and rebuild their lives. Substance dependence can affect an individual’s health, family relationships and livelihood.
The journey of Imran Khan
(name changed)
, a 33-year-old self-employed AC mechanic from Gorakhpur district of Uttar Pradesh, illustrates the role of rehabilitation support in helping a person move towards recovery and financial independence.
Imran’s struggle with addiction began at the age of 12, when he started smoking cigarettes under peer pressure. Over time, his dependence expanded to tobacco, gutkha, alcohol, smack, injectable drugs and cannabis. His physical and mental well-being deteriorated, and he experienced behavioural difficulties and financial dependence. His substance dependence affected several aspects of his life, including his relationships, livelihood and social standing.
Imran belonged to a financially disadvantaged family with two brothers and six sisters. His addiction placed emotional and financial strain on the household, while social stigma and strained relationships added to the family’s difficulties. Although he had learned AC repair and other mechanical work, much of his income was spent on substances, preventing him from achieving financial stability. His family remained deeply concerned about his health, and his father experienced heart complications that required bypass surgery. Despite these hardships, his family continued to support him and encouraged him to seek treatment.
On 22 October 2019, Imran received support at Punarjanm Integrated Rehabilitation Centre for Addicts (IRCA), Sonbarasa, Gorakhpur, operated by Basudev Tiwari Sewa Sansthan. He received medical treatment and detoxification support, psychological counselling, motivational therapy and structured rehabilitation. The centre also provided medicines, safe accommodation, nutritious food, emotional support, family counselling and regular monitoring, along with relapse-prevention guidance and livelihood support.
With professional care, continued encouragement and family involvement, Imran developed greater confidence and self-control. He completed a three-month rehabilitation programme and overcame his substance dependence. The intervention helped him focus on his recovery, restore family relationships and return to productive work.
Today, Imran leads a drug-free life and works independently as an AC mechanic, undertaking other mechanical jobs as well. He earns approximately ₹30,000–₹40,000 per month and contributes to household expenses, improving his family’s financial position. His recovery has also helped him regain his family’s trust and respect within society.
Imran’s experience highlights the importance of accessible treatment, psychological support, structured rehabilitation and family involvement in supporting recovery and social reintegration. The assistance provided through Punarjanm IRCA has helped him rebuild his livelihood and move towards a more stable and independent future.

to facilitate the comprehensive rehabilitation, socio-economic empowerment and social reintegration of persons engaged in begging.
The Official further said the Scheme is currently being implemented in 216 cities across 33 States and Union Territories, with a focus on restoring dignity, promoting self-reliance and enabling sustainable social and economic reintegration. To date, 45,073 persons have been identified under the Scheme, out of which 13,134 have received rehabilitation support, the official added.
The official emphasised that the Scheme goes beyond merely removing persons from the streets and adopts a holistic, rehabilitation-oriented approach to address the underlying vulnerabilities that lead to begging. The interventions encompass identification and profiling, rescue and outreach, counselling, shelter and essential services, healthcare, education, skill development, livelihood support and convergence with social security schemes.
To strengthen implementation and ensure measurable outcomes, the Ministry has introduced several reforms. These include a mobile application for comprehensive surveys and profiling of persons engaged in begging, along with a portal for digital monitoring; model guidelines for transforming beggars’ homes into dignified rehabilitation and care facilities in accordance with the directions of the Hon’ble Supreme Court; and a Begging-Free City Framework with clearly defined and measurable Key Performance Indicators (KPIs).
Other key measures include convergence with social security and social welfare schemes to facilitate access to entitlements and essential services, as well as performance-based incentives to encourage cities to make measurable progress towards achieving Begging-Free status. Collectively, these initiatives seek to establish an outcome-oriented, accountable and convergence-driven rehabilitation ecosystem.
The official further stated that focused efforts are underway to strengthen rehabilitation services, expand livelihood opportunities, improve access to social security and facilitate sustainable reintegration, thereby advancing Delhi towards the goal of
‘Bhiksha Vritti Mukt Delhi’
.
He said Delhi was among the seven cities selected during the pilot phase of the Scheme in FY 2021–22. The Scheme is now operational across all 14 districts/cities of Delhi, reflecting the expansion of efforts towards comprehensive rehabilitation and social reintegration.
During the programme, a large number of beneficiaries identified and supported under the SMILE–Beggary Scheme will be felicitated. They will also be provided with skill-building and rehabilitation kits to support their transition towards self-reliance and sustainable livelihoods.
Towards 100 Begging-Free Cities by 2031
To achieve the target of
100 Begging-Free Cities by 2031
, the Ministry underscores the importance of coordinated and sustained efforts by the Central and State Governments, urban local bodies, district administrations, non-governmental organisations, voluntary organisations and local communities. Sustainable rehabilitation requires a collective commitment to addressing vulnerabilities, ensuring access to essential services and creating opportunities for dignified and independent living.
Under the SMILE–Beggary Scheme for FY 2026–31, the Government has set an ambitious target of making 100 cities Begging-Free. The strategy is supported by measurable KPIs, digital monitoring, innovation and inter-departmental convergence to strengthen implementation and track progress.
The Delhi programme will reaffirm the collective resolve to accelerate progress towards this national goal. It will highlight how convergence, accountability, compassion and community participation can translate the vision of
‘Bhiksha Vritti Mukt Bharat’
into a sustainable reality while advancing Delhi towards becoming
‘Bhiksha Vritti Mukt Delhi’

title: BRICS Traditional and Indigenous Demonstration Games 2026 Celebrate Sporting Heritage and Cultural Diversity in Ahmedabad
subtitle:
Union Minister of Youth & Affairs Dr. Mansukh Mandaviya said that India is placing sport at the centre of nation-building by investing in future-ready sports infrastructure.

Dr. Mandaviya calls for BRICS repository, expert exchanges, and periodic demonstrations of traditional and indigenous sports

Union Sports Minister highlights traditional sport as a vehicle for youth development, inclusion, cultural understanding, and international cooperation
ministry: Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                12 OCT 2026 4:07PM by PIB Delhi
content:
Ahmedabad, October 12, 2026:
The BRICS Traditional and Indigenous Demonstration Games 2026 were held on Monday, October 12, 2026 at the Veer Savarkar Sports Complex, Naranpura, Ahmedabad, Gujarat.
The day-long event brought together dignitaries, country delegations, athletes, practitioners, technical officials, and partner institutions to celebrate the sporting heritage, cultural diversity, and people-to-people connections of BRICS countries.
Declaring the games open, Union Minister of Youth & Affairs Dr. Mansukh Mandaviya said that India is placing sport at the centre of nation-building by investing in future-ready sports infrastructure.
The Union Minister inaugurated the event in the esteemed presence of Shri Harsh Sanghavi, Hon'ble Deputy Chief Minister, Gujarat.
Addressing the representatives from the 10 BRICS nations and other attendees, the Union Sports Minister highlighted India’s commitment towards building a sporting nation.
He said, “India is placing sport at the centre of nation-building. Under the leadership of Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi, India is transforming its sporting ecosystem by creating opportunities from the playground to the podium.
“Guided by a comprehensive 360-degree approach, including grassroots participation, talent identification, coaching, sports science, infrastructure development, athlete welfare and international exposure, India is building a sustainable sporting ecosystem for the future,” said Dr. Mandaviya.
“To support this transformation, we have committed nearly 3.76 billion US Dollar as part of our Khelo India initiative.”
Dr. Mandaviya further proposed three practical areas of cooperation among BRICS nations to preserve and promote traditional and indigenous sports.
“BRICS Traditional and Indigenous Games provide a platform to showcase not only how a sport is played, but also the history, values and cultural context that make each tradition unique. As we take this initiative forward, India proposes three practical areas of cooperation,” said Dr. Mandaviya.
“First, we should work towards creating a voluntary BRICS Repository of Traditional and Indigenous Sports, documenting their history, cultural significance, rules, equipment and field-of-play requirements.”
“Second, we should encourage exchanges among practitioners, coaches, researchers, educational institutions and cultural experts across BRICS countries,” continued the Union Sports Minister.
“Third, we should explore the periodic demonstration of traditional and indigenous sports at future BRICS sporting events,” he added.
Dr. Mandaviya further went on to describe how India is taking major strides towards making sports a way of life through the FiT India Movement.
“Through the Fit India Movement, we are promoting fitness as a way of life,” he said.
“Our ‘Sundays on Cycle’ campaign has seen tremendous success with more than 5 Million people coming to cycle across more than 3 lakh locations every Sunday. So far, 94 editions of the ‘Sundays on Cycle’ have been conducted across India.”
The 10 participating BRICS nations demonstrated a number of their indigenous sporting traditions at the Veer Savarkar Sports Complex:
Belarus:
Gorodki
Bolivia:
Lucha de Cholitas, Tinku, Rayuela, Trompo, Cachinas and Carrera de Sacos
Brazil:
Zarabatana (Indigenous Blowpipe), Corrida de Toras (Log Race), Brazilian Para-Jiu-jitsu and Capoeira
China:
Wushu, Lion Dance and Health Qigong
India:
Mallakhamb, Yogasana, Kalaripayattu
Iran:
Zoorkhaneh, Haft Sang and Ghanieh
Kazakhstan:
Asyk Atu, Togyzkumalak and Qazaq Kuresi
Russia:
Gorodki and Sambo
South Africa:
Kgati and Iintonga
United Arab Emirates:
Al Tabbah
The demonstrations were complemented by cultural presentations and audience-engagement activities. Participating teams were felicitated at the conclusion of the programme.
The Games provided a common platform for BRICS countries to present the history, values, cultural context, and practice of their traditional sports.
The event reinforced the importance of preserving community knowledge while modernising sport, expanding inclusive participation, and deepening friendship and cooperation across the BRICS family.

The nationwide initiative covered 1,469 locations across 34 States, with participation from over 3.65 lakh youth and citizens, reinforcing the collective commitment towards building a drug-free India.
The initiative aimed to strengthen grassroots youth engagement, raise awareness about the harmful effects of substance abuse and encourage young people to take an active role in preventing drug abuse. The Neighbourhood Youth Parliaments, organised at the block level, featured discussions on the challenges associated with substance abuse, strategies to translate awareness into action and inspiring stories of change, motivating young people to become advocates for a healthy and drug-free society.
The programmes featured a range of youth-led activities, including the Nasha Mukt Yuva Pledge, slogan-writing competitions, signature campaigns, debates, Nukkad Nataks and interactive discussions. These activities encouraged participants to adopt healthy lifestyles and spread awareness about the importance of preventing substance abuse. The Yuva Melas were organised in collaboration with spiritual organisations, university associations and industry associations, including Heartfulness, Project Point, CIPU, ASSOCHAM, FICCI and Brahma Kumaris, strengthening the reach and impact of the campaign through multi-stakeholder participation.
The initiative also witnessed the participation of public representatives, with six representatives, including one Member of Parliament and five Members of Legislative Assemblies, attending the programmes. A total of 4,552 activities were organised, and 4,568 slogans were collected, reflecting the extensive engagement of participants in promoting the message of a Nasha Mukt Bharat.
The nationwide mobilisation under the 100 Weeks Campaign highlights the role of collective action, community participation and youth leadership in addressing substance abuse. Through Neighbourhood Youth Parliaments and Yuva Melas, MY Bharat continues to encourage young people to take responsibility for social change and contribute towards realising the vision of Nasha Mukt Yuva for Viksit Bharat.

title: Five Years of PM GatiShakti: Transforming India’s Infrastructure Planning
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                12 OCT 2026 1:49PM by PIB Delhi
content:
PM GatiShakti National Master Plan (PMGS-NMP)
has evolved from a national infrastructure mapping platform into a wider planning framework. It brings together Ministries, States and infrastructure networks through a GIS-based platform to support integrated planning and project coordination.
Today, it covers 58 Central Ministries and Departments and all 36 States and Union Territories.
Infrastructure As The Engine of Viksit Bharat
India is building infrastructure at a scale that requires coordination across sectors and modes of transport. Roads, railways, ports, airports, waterways and utilities often intersect across the same regions. Planning these networks together can help in cost and time savings, coordinate projects and use existing infrastructure more efficiently. This created a need for an approach that integrates different infrastructure networks into a common planning framework.
To address this need, the
PM GatiShakti National Master Plan was launched on 13 October 2021.
It brought data from different ministries, States and Union Territories onto a common Geographic Information System (GIS)-based platform. PM GatiShakti enables planners to view infrastructure, geographic features, economic zones and other relevant data together, supporting data-driven planning and decision-making for infrastructure projects. Five years on, this approach has grown into a nationwide planning framework.
PM GatiShakti At A Glance
PM GatiShakti is guided by
six principles
that seek to make infrastructure planning more integrated, efficient, and coordinated. This includes integrated development, multimodal infrastructure, last mile connectivity, expedited land acquisition, minimised clearances and reduced ecological impact.
Key features of PM GatiShakti include:
Do You Know?
PM Gati Shakti incorporates infrastructure schemes from various Ministries and State Governments, such as Bharatmala, Sagarmala, inland waterways, dry/land ports, and UDAN.
Seven Infrastructure Engines:
Roads, Railways, Ports, Waterways, Airports, Mass Transport and Logistics Infrastructure form the core sectors of the plan.
Whole-of-Government Planning:
The National Master Plan covers
58 Central Ministries and Departments and all 36 States and Union Territories,
enabling infrastructure proposals to be planned and assessed across sectors.
Integrated Digital Planning:
The NMP brings together infrastructure, and geospatial information on a common GIS-based platform, supporting spatial planning and decision-making.
Wider Data Access:
The
PM GatiShakti Public
platform provides access to
230 approved datasets
, enabling site suitability analysis, connectivity mapping, alignment planning and compliance checks.
Data Layers:
Over 23,493 data layers, as of 12 October 2026,
bring infrastructure and other relevant information onto the common GIS-based platform.
ITLA: Strengthening Integrated Transport Planning
Complementing PM GatiShakti, the Union Cabinet recently approved the establishment of the Integrated Transport & Logistics Authority (ITLA). The Authority will focus on long-term transport planning and coordination.
ITLA will prepare a
National Transport Master Plan
with a planning horizon of ten years or more. It will assess sectoral and annual transport plans, and undertake technical appraisal of projects costing ₹500 crore or more. The authority will also monitor their implementation. It will also develop a National Transport Data Repository (NTDR) by integrating information from sources such as FASTag, Vahan, and GSTN e-way bills.
How GatiShakti Works: From Coordination to Project Planning
PM GatiShakti has a
three-tier institutional framework
comprising the following:
Empowered Group of Secretaries (EGoS)
: Chaired by the Cabinet Secretary, the EGoS oversees the implementation of PM GatiShakti and reviews, considers and approves changes in the Master Plan.
Network Planning Group (NPG):
The NPG brings together the Heads of Network Planning Divisions from infrastructure Ministries and Departments. It examines infrastructure proposals and ensures unified planning, integration and optimisation. It also monitors developments under the National Master Plan for project planning.
Technical Support Unit (TSU):
The TSU comprises domain and subject-matter experts who support the evaluation process. It assists the Logistics Division in performing its role as the PM GatiShakti Secretariat.
As of
11 August 2026
, the NPG had
evaluated 396 infrastructure projects
with a total estimated cost of about
₹18.66 lakh crore
. Of these,
256 projects had been sanctioned, of which 198 were under implementation
.  The institutional framework is supported by a digital platform that provides planners with
geospatial data, satellite imagery and analytical tools
.
Gati Shakti Vishwavidyalaya: Building Expertise for Integrated Infrastructure Planning
Gati Shakti Vishwavidyalaya (GSV) is a first-of-its-kind university focused exclusively on the transport and logistics sectors. Established in 2022, the university brings together education, executive training and research across transport-related disciplines.
GSV supports the PM GatiShakti National Master Plan and the National Logistics Policy (2022) through specialised education, training and research.  GSV serves as a nodal agency for developing and delivering courses on both initiatives. The collaboration also envisages knowledge centres to share best practices and promote research and innovation in logistics. As of July 2026, the university had trained more than 2.4 lakh officers through courses designed for PM GatiShakti. The university is also expanding its focus on applied research for integrated transport planning, alongside specialised areas such as maritime transport, bridge and tunnel engineering, and defence logistics.
From Data To Decisions: How Digital Planning Is Helping Planners
The NMP brings together
GIS-based data on infrastructure, geographic features, and demography
on a common platform. Economic zones are also mapped alongside multimodal connectivity infrastructure to support integrated infrastructure planning. This enables planners to view different infrastructure networks and relevant geographic information together while planning projects.
The platform combines
spatial planning and analytical tools
with mechanisms for updating and integrating data. It can support activities such as adding project information, measuring proximity, identifying Go/No-Go areas (areas where development may be restricted) and obtaining clearances.
Mapping Infrastructure and Infrastructure Nodes
The PM GatiShakti NMP maps
economic, social and logistics nodes alongside multimodal connectivity infrastructure
. This brings infrastructure linkages and the surrounding development context into the planning process. The platform helps identify
infrastructure linkages required to support economic zones and development projects
, as well as
missing connectivity gaps
that can affect the seamless movement of people, goods and services.
Economic zones such as
textile and pharmaceutical clusters, defence corridors, electronic parks, industrial corridors, fishing clusters and agri zones
are mapped to support integrated infrastructure planning.
Example:
Khagaria–Purnea
corridor in Bihar. The upgraded corridor is planned to connect five PM GatiShakti Economic Nodes, including a textile cluster, Mega Food Parks and fishing/seafood parks, along with 11 logistics nodes. The planned connectivity is intended to facilitate faster movement of goods and passengers across the region.
Connecting Logistics Systems
Unified Logistics Interface Platform (ULIP) enables API-based integration of government logistics systems, while the Logistics Data Bank (LDB) provides real-time tracking of EXIM container movement. Together, they strengthen digital information exchange and visibility across the logistics ecosystem. As of July 2026,
ULIP connected 46 government systems across 12 Central Ministries through 142 APIs.
Opening Geospatial Data to Wider Users
The digital ecosystem has also expanded beyond government users. In October 2025, the PM GatiShakti NMP platform was opened to the private sector through a
Query-Based Analytics Mechanism developed by Bhaskaracharya National Institute for Space Applications and Geo-informatics (BISAG-N).
The platform provides regulated access to selected non-sensitive datasets for infrastructure planning and investment decisions.
The platform currently provides access to 230 approved datasets covering physical and social infrastructure assets. Users can undertake site
suitability analysis, connectivity mapping, alignment planning and compliance checks
, and generate analytical reports.
From Data to Monitoring
The digital platform also supports the tracking of project progress and updating of infrastructure data. The PM GatiShakti NMP Dashboard provides multi-sector reporting to track progress and derive actionable insights. The
Data Uploading and Management System (DUMS)
enables decentralised and real-time data ownership and updating.
The overall approach uses
geospatial data, satellite imagery and API integration
to support data-driven decision-making, planning and optimisation of infrastructure development.
PM GatiShakti in Action
Pune–Bengaluru Expressway
: The
699 km Expressway,
with expected completion in 2027–28, will connect industrial and economic clusters across Maharashtra and Karnataka. These include automobile and white-goods factories, pharmaceutical clusters, special economic zones, and defence corridors. The project connects
15 National Highways, 25 State Highways and 6 railway stations
, enabling multimodal connectivity. Using the PM GatiShakti NMP platform, the alignment was revised to reduce forest land overlap by
19%
. The project is expected to reduce travel time by
7–8 hours
. It will also save approximately
16 crore litres of fuel annually
and reduce carbon emissions by around
39 crore kg
.
Jogighopa Multimodal Logistics Park, Assam
:  The
Jogighopa Multimodal Logistics Park
is located on the northern banks of the Brahmaputra in Assam. It is designed to enable seamless cargo movement across
road, rail and inland waterways
in the Northeast. PM GatiShakti was used for integrated planning and demand analysis. A four-lane bridge under construction across the Brahmaputra between
Dhubri and Phulbari
is planned to reduce the travel distance from
205 km to 20 km
and travel time from about
seven hours to 30 minutes
.
Green Energy Corridor: Ladakh–Haryana:
The project, recommended by NPG under PM GatiShakti, will enable
evacuation and grid integration of 13 GW of renewable energy through a 5 GW transmission system
. It includes a
480-km HVDC transmission line between Pang in Ladakh and Kaithal in Haryana
, with 5 GW HVDC terminals at both ends. The transmission system will pass through Himachal Pradesh and Punjab before connecting with the national grid at Kaithal. The project is targeted for completion by
FY2029–30
.
Building a Connected Infrastructure Future
Five years after its launch, PM GatiShakti has evolved from a national infrastructure planning initiative into a wider digital planning ecosystem. Its expansion across Ministries, States, districts and new infrastructure domains is creating a more integrated approach to planning India's next generation of infrastructure.

title: NHRC, India organises a National Conference on the theme ‘Water as the Elixir of Life: Advancing Human Dignity through the Right to Water’ on its 33rd Foundation Day in New Delhi
subtitle:
Emphasising action must begin immediately, NHRC Chairperson, Justice V. Ramasubramanian says, the present generation owes a responsibility to preserve natural resources for future generations

The Conference deliberates on various human rights dimensions of water security, conservation and sustainable management
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                12 OCT 2026 7:12PM by PIB Delhi
content:
The National Human Rights Commission (NHRC), India organised a National Conference on the theme ‘Water as the Elixir of Life: Advancing Human Dignity through the Right to Water’ at Vigyan Bhawan, New Delhi today, as part of the celebrations marking its 33rd Foundation Day. The Conference brought together representatives of government institutions, development organisations and other stakeholders to deliberate on the human rights dimensions of access to safe drinking water, sustainable management of water resources, rejuvenation of water bodies, community participation and the need to strengthen institutional mechanisms for ensuring water security.
Addressing the first session on ‘Water conservation, sustainability and community participation’ Shri Brijendra Swaroop, Executive Director (Projects), National Mission for Clean Ganga, Ministry of Jal Shakti emphasised that non-discriminatory access to adequate, safe and affordable water is fundamental to human dignity. Outlining the Namami Gange Programme, he highlighted its Integrated River Basin Management approach and the objectives of ensuring Nirmal Dhara (unpolluted flow), Aviral Dhara (continuous flow) and protection of the Ganga’s geological and ecological integrity. The programme comprises 527 projects with a sanctioned cost of approximately Rs 43,326 crore, covering pollution abatement, ecological restoration, biodiversity conservation, community participation, research and livelihood enhancement.
He stressed the need for comprehensive wastewater management, maintenance of ecological flows, protection of floodplains, wetland restoration and biodiversity conservation. Referring to improvements in water quality in several stretches of the Ganga, he observed that the success of rejuvenation efforts should be assessed through environmental outcomes, including water quality, biodiversity and ecosystem functioning, rather than expenditure or the number of completed projects alone. He called for scientific mapping of water bodies, catchment-based planning, institutional convergence and community participation, emphasising that conservation must precede restoration.
Shri Yugal Kishore Joshi, Programme Director, NITI Aayog highlighted India’s water-security challenges, noting that the country has approximately 4% of the world’s freshwater resources but nearly 18% of its population. Per capita water availability has declined to approximately 1,300–1,400 cubic metres annually, below the water-stress threshold of 1,700 cubic metres. He emphasised integrating traditional water-harvesting practices with modern scientific methods, strengthening Gram Panchayats, preparing water budgets and addressing encroachment.
Citing a community-led initiative covering approximately 800 villages, in which water-body rejuvenation had been completed in 731 villages at an approximate cost of Rs. 3 lakh per water body, he highlighted the importance of community labour and productive use of excavated silt. He called for stronger local institutions, improved monitoring and wider replication of successful conservation initiatives.
Ms.Anjali Makhija, CEO and Trustee, S M Sehgal Foundation highlighted the importance of collaboration among communities, government, development organisations, academia and other stakeholders in addressing water and agricultural challenges. She outlined the Foundation’s work on groundwater recharge, supplementary surface-water storage, rainwater harvesting in schools, water quality and climate-smart, water-efficient agriculture, including drip and sprinkler irrigation and laser land levelling.
She emphasised the role of women’s groups and village development committees in identifying priorities, contributing resources and maintaining water structures. Stressing the need to work in coordination with local and district administrations, she advocated combining traditional knowledge with scientific expertise through GIS mapping, soil-moisture and water-quality monitoring as well as third-party assessments. She also called for affordable and accessible technology, greater philanthropic and CSR investment in water and agriculture, besides the development of a scientifically designed water-credit system.
Dr. Rajendra Singh, Chairperson, Tarun Bharat Sanghemphasised that water has its own rights and that rivers must remain nirmal (pure) and aviral (flowing uninterruptedly), with their ecological integrity protected alongside the human right to water. Reflecting on India’s natural wealth and its decline, he highlighted his experience of restoring 23 rivers through community participation, traditional water-conservation practices and ecological restoration.
He stressed that the right to water must go hand in hand with the responsibility to protect rivers and their natural ecosystems. Emphasising that knowledge and advocacy must translate into meaningful environmental action, he called for drawing upon traditional wisdom to conserve natural resources, restore rivers and preserve ecological balance for future generations.
Addressing the second session on ‘Strengthening drinking-water services and local governance’ Shri Ashok K. K. Meena, Secretary, Department of Drinking Water and Sanitation, Ministry of Jal Shakti emphasised that safe drinking water is integral to human dignity, public health and the right to life under Article 21 of the Constitution.
Referring to the Jal Jeevan Mission, launched in 2019, he stated that approximately 82% of the planned water-connection infrastructure had been created. He noted that approximately 25% of blocks were in critical, semi-critical or over-exploited groundwater categories. Surface water-dependent schemes had increased from 15% to 48%, while groundwater-dependent schemes had declined from 85% to 52%.
He called for village-level water budgeting, source sustainability, digital monitoring and stronger Gram Panchayats and Village Water and Sanitation Committees. Highlighting water-quality surveillance, he noted that approximately 2.4 million women had been trained to use field-testing kits and upload data for remedial action. He stressed interdepartmental convergence and referred to completing infrastructure under Jal Jeevan Mission 2.0 by December 2028, ensuring safe, reliable and sustainable drinking-water services.
Shri Uma Shankar Pandey, noted social worker, farmer and groundwater conservationist emphasised the vital importance of water conservation through collective stakeholder efforts. He highlighted concerns regarding the commercialisation and wastage of water and stressed that ensuring access to safe drinking water is a shared responsibility of the Government and the community. He underscored the need for water literacy, community participation and revival of traditional water-management practices. Using the example of a little bird attempting to extinguish a forest fire, he highlighted the significance of individual contributions. Emphasising the importance of awareness creation, he asserted that building a New Bharat must begin with individual responsibility. He reiterated his slogan, “Khetmein med, med par ped”, advocating tree plantation on agricultural field bundsas a sustainable water-conservation practice.
Shri Anand Shekhar, CEO, Water Aid India appreciated the NHRC, India’s focus on water as a fundamental human right. He stressed that every household tap must be supported by a sustainable water source to ensure reliable access. Recalling that sanitation coverage in India was below 20% in 2014, he highlighted the progress achieved in eliminating open defecation and extending sustainable sanitation services to all rural households within five years through political leadership, public investment and community participation.
He noted that approximately 86% of households now have access to drinking-water services through functional household tap connections. He also highlighted the opportunity presented by the allocation of approximately Rs. 8 lakh crore placed at the disposal of Gram Panchayats, of which 50% earmarked for water and sanitation, enabling nearly 2.5 lakh Gram Panchayats to strengthen service delivery. Emphasising source sustainability under the Jal Jeevan Mission, he called for political and administrative ownership, adequate public financing, inter-ministerial coordination, multi-stakeholder partnerships and greater community mobilisation. He underlined that the objective must go beyond coverage to ensure “water for everyone and for always” through reliable, quality and sustainable drinking-water services.
In the concluding session, Justice V. Ramasubramanian, Chairperson, NHRC expressed gratitude to the participants and highlighted the significance of the PanchBhoota, the five elements of nature, in sustaining life and maintaining ecological balance. Reflecting on the properties of water, he appreciated the collaborative approach to conservation advocated by the panellists and stressed collective efforts and stakeholder participation. He highlighted the contradiction between reverence and action, observing that society often fails to protect what it reveres, citing women and water as examples. He called for responsible behaviour and sustained conservation efforts to bridge this gap.
The Chairperson emphasised that conservation efforts must begin immediately, noting that the present generation has benefited from the efforts and sacrifices of its ancestors and has a responsibility to preserve natural resources for future generations. He underscored the cumulative impact of individual and collective efforts, stressing that conservation initiatives require a long-term vision, even when results take decades to emerge. He called for timely, sustained and collaborative action to safeguard water resources for present and future generations.
Shri Piyush Goyal, Secretary General, NHRC summarised the deliberations of the two thematic sessions. He emphasised the urgency of addressing climate change and severe groundwater depletion through decentralised, community-led governance involving Gram Panchayats, village-level water and sanitation committees, women’s groups and civil society. He stressed that, although significant ground-level work remained, close coordination among government agencies, civil society and local communities would help ensure a positive and sustainable way forward.
Shri Samir Kumar, Joint Secretary, NHRC, India delivered the vote of thanks expressing gratitude to the Chief Guest, the Chief Justice of India, for accepting the invitation and sharing his insights.
He also thanked the NHRC Chairperson and Members for their guidance and leadership and representatives of Ministries, government departments, civil society organisations and other participants for their valuable contributions. He acknowledged the efforts of all those involved in organising the conference and reiterated the collective commitment to the promotion and protection of human rights.

title: NHRC, India celebrates its 33rd Foundation Day in New Delhi
subtitle:
Addressing the gathering as the Chief Guest, Chief Justice of India, Justice Surya Kant lauds the NHRC’s work over the years. Describes the Commission as a guiding light to those adrift in the darkness

Says, SHRCs have a significant role to play, given their proximity to the ground where human rights violation occurs

Commending NHRC for organising the National Conference on Water as the Elixir of Life, the CJI says, the right to water must be understood not only as a right of the present but as a responsibility towards the future

NHRC Chairperson, Justice V. Ramasubramanian says, given the complex challenges facing the world today, human rights institutions throughout the world need to reinvent themselves to continue to be relevant
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                12 OCT 2026 6:33PM by PIB Delhi
content:
The National Human Rights Commission (NHRC), India today organised a function and National Conference on the theme ‘Water as the Elixir of Life: Advancing Human Dignity through the Right to Water’ to celebrate its 33rd Foundation Day at Vigyan Bhawan, New Delhi. The Commission was set up on 12th October 1993. Addressing the function as the Chief Guest, Chief Justice of India, Justice Surya Kant said that the Constitution of India has made extensive promises to every citizen, including for dignity, equality, liberty and justice. These words in the preamble are among the finest ever written and they must be observed day after day in the field, in the lockup, in the hospital ward and in the village at the end of the road.
Lauding the NHRC’s work over the years, Justice Kant said that people sometimes say that “the Commission can only recommend and cannot command, but I would offer an alternative perspective. Picture, for a moment, a solitary lighthouse standing steadfast at the edge of society’s vast, restless sea. Its purpose is not to steal the waves of injustice but to cast a guiding light for those adrift in the darkness.” He said that Human Rights Commissions must investigate complaints, identify systemic failures and ensure that concerns which may otherwise remain invisible receive institutional attention. Civil society can bring ground realities to the forefront while international institutions can contribute scientific knowledge, experience and cooperation.
Justice Surya Kant said that the true measure of a human rights institution is therefore not only the number of cases it decides but whether it can be heard by those who are least able to make themselves heard. This is where the Human Rights Commissions, particularly the State Human Rights Commissions (SHRCs), have a significant role to play. In a country as large and diverse as India, the experience of rights is often determined not in the capital, but in a remote village, a particular neighbourhood or even the household. The National Commission can set standards and draw attention to larger patterns, but State Commissions are often closer to the ground where violations occur. They can hear a complaint in the language in which it is made, reach the place where it has occurred and understand the local circumstances in which it has taken place. That proximity gives them not merely an administrative advantage, but a life-altering responsibility.
He also commended the Commission for pairing the celebration with the National Conference on ‘Water as the Elixir of Life.’ He said that the right to water must therefore be understood not only as a right of the present but also as a responsibility towards the future.
Justice Kant said that India itself has made astronomical efforts to expand access to drinking water, including through the provisions of household tap connections in rural areas. That progress deserves commendation, but the next question must be a more demanding one. Is the water safe, reliable and available when the family needs it? Therefore, “the Government must build and maintain the systems through which water reaches people. Courts must intervene when constitutional rights are violated.”
He also appreciated the Commission for the launch of the NHRC, India mobile application and the move towards digitisation of its records. He said that this App make the Commission more accessible to those who have traditionally found it difficult to approach formal institutions.
Before this, thanking the CJI for accepting the invitation to be the Chief Guest for the Foundation Day, NHRC Chairperson, Justice V. Ramasubramanian said that “the office of the CJI has become the single most important, the most powerful, the most vibrant, at the same time, the most vulnerable office of the country which is put to the test of fire (Agni Pariksha), every day, nay, every minute, not necessarily by sacred souls at all times.”
The Chairperson said that “there can be no disagreement on the fact that the world today is a much better place to live than it was hundred years ago. But at the same time, the challenges that we face today are more complex than ever. Therefore, it is the necessity of time that human rights institutions throughout the world reinvent themselves to continue to be relevant.”
Justice Ramasubramanian said that the poorest half of the world’s population is responsible for only 14% of global CO₂ emissions. The world’s richest 10% are responsible for half of all emissions. It is no coincidence that climate and wealth are so closely linked, as they essentially share a common origin: fossil capitalism. Fossil fuels are the source of humanity’s extraordinary progress over the past two centuries but also the source of the extraordinary problems facing us today.
He said that until a few decades ago, our approach to human rights issues was normally two- dimensional. We presumed that it was citizen versus State. But it is not so anymore. Non-State actors now play a huge role, especially after the digital revolution has happened. Today, in the digital world, our opinions can be manipulated, our thought processes can be influenced and our activities, both physical and mental, can be monitored. Therefore, it is time for us, especially when we celebrate NHRC Foundation Day, to take a pledge to reinvent ourselves to face new challenges, reaffirm our commitment to the cause of promotion and protection of human rights and re-engineer our personalities to improve our delivery system.
Earlier, NHRC Member, Justice (Dr.) Bidyut Ranjan Sarangi said that the Commission is committed to promoting and protecting human rights of all including the right to dignity and equality in accordance with the law and the Constitution. In the 33 years of NHRC, there may have been some ups and downs, but it remains committed to its responsibility to serve the cause of human rights. It has expanded its outreach to the doorsteps of the victims of human rights violations through its open hearing and camp sittings.
NHRC Member, Smt. Vijaya Bharathi Sayani said that the concept of human rights is deeply rooted in ancient Indian civilisation, which is also reflected in the Constitution of the country. Quoting Rigvedas and Upanishads, she highlighted that India’s ancient scriptures guided us on how to live together with mutual respect and protect human dignity and wellbeing of all through dialogue and collective strength. Therefore, she said that we must take pride in our heritage and work as equal stakeholders for the protection of eights of girls, children and women, among other vulnerable groups.
In his opening remarks, NHRC Secretary General, Shri Piyush Goyal gave an overview of various dimensions of the Commission’s work towards promoting and protecting life. He said that the subjects of human rights are evolving with time. Climate change and digital world are throwing new challenges. He said that as part of its 33rd Foundation celebration, the Commission has organised a National Conference on the theme ‘Water as the Elixir of Life: Advancing Human Dignity through the Right to Water.’ The two technical sessions include ‘Protection and Restoration of Water Bodies: Safeguarding the Foundation of the Right to Water’ and ‘Protecting Drinking Water Sources: Ensuring Safe and Sustainable Access to Water for All.’ He expressed the hope that the deliberations would result in meaningful recommendations.
